newsitem.title: UK: S&P rating agency sees EMU positive for credit.
newsitem.headline: S&P rating agency sees EMU positive for credit.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Monday the net effect of European and Monetary Union (EMU) should be broadly positive for credit trends within European companies without triggering substantial changes in corporate ratings.

Banks and retailers are among the potential losers from EMU, the agency said. Credit quality for sovereign countries joining EMU would remain strong, it said, adding that it did not expect any initial rating changes for countries that did not join.
On the corporate side, a survival-of-the-fittest regime would prevail under EMU, Standard & Poor's (S&P) said.

"Greater competition fostered by a larger and deeper domestic market and greater price and cost transparency are likely to benefit successful and efficient companies," said Rupert Atkinson, director of corporate ratings at S&P.
S&P said that the outlook was generally positive for corporate credit trends because the universe of rated European companies was skewed towards this type of efficient company.
"A number of other factors are likely to have a beneficial impact on some corporates," S&P said in a statement.

"The cost of capital for corporates in some countries may be reduced if interest and inflation rates stabilise at lower than the weighted average of the participating countries, although interest rates may rise for countries at the heart of Europe."
Borrowing should generally be easier in a larger and more liquid capital market and weaker credits should have easier access to the capital markets, it said.

"The most straightforward benefits of a single currency stem from the reduction in cross-border financial transaction costs within the EMU zone, via the elimination of foreign exchange risks and costs," said Atkinson.
A number of costs and drawbacks offset the broadly positive factors associated with EMU, S&P said.
"It seems fairly clear that European economic growth rates will be impaired in the rush to meet public debt and budget deficit criteria stipulated in the Maastricht treaty."
S&P said this was expected to have a short term negative impact on profitability.

"More significantly, corporates will incur substantial one-off and transitional costs in switching to the euro, in information technology, accounting and financial management, tax, legal and payment systems, marketing and product planning."
S&P said the retailing sector was likely to be particularly badly affected.
S&P also said EMU would put earnings in the banking sector under pressure as banks suffered the permanent loss of revenues from certain currency transactions.

"Another problem facing companies in countries that don't join EMU in the first wave is that they will incur many of the costs involved without initially reaping all of the benefits of the single currency," the agency said.
